4.In MATRIXX INITIATIVES, INC. v. SIRACUSANO, 563 U.S. 27, 131 S.Ct. 1309, 179 L.Ed.2d 398 (2011), the Supreme Court addressed
two separate pleading questions. The first involved the pleading of materiality under Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and applied
the plausibility standard of Twombly and Iqbal. The second involved the pleading of scienter, which was assessed under the PSLRA. For both, the
Court held that an allegation of statistical significance was not required to show that the omitted statements—in this case, adverse pharmaceutical event
reports—were material to the reasonable investor and that defendant acted with the requisite state of mind. Matrixx has generated a number of
important questions, including the relationship between the plausibility and the PSLRA pleading standards. See Steinberg & Gomez-Cornejo, Blurring
the Lines Between Pleading Doctrines: The Enhanced Rule 8(a)(2) Plausibility Pleading Standard Converges with the Heightened Fraud Pleading
Standards under Rule 9(b) and the PSLRA, 30 Rev.Litig. 1 (2010).
5. Many empirical studies have tried to assess the PSLRA’s effect on securities markets, in terms of firm value, litigation practice, judicial filings,
and disposition rates. In the first decade after the PSLRA’s enactment, the number of securities class action filings did not decrease, but the cases
involved higher-value claims and took a longer period of time to settle. Beginning around 2005, filing rates began to decline. See Choi & Thompson,
Securities Litigation and Its Lawyers: Changes During the First Decade after the PSLRA, 106 Colum.L.Rev. 148 (2006). In 2012, the number of
filings declined to 152, a 19 percent drop from the previous year and 21 percent below the average number of filings in the period 1997–2011. See
Cornerstone Research, Securities Class Action Filings: 2012 Year in Review (Jan. 2013). Moreover, district courts appeared to have granted an
increased percentage of motions to dismiss, and in almost every case filed under the PSLRA, defendant moved to dismiss the action. See Wunderlich,
The Importance of the Prefiling Phase for Securities-Fraud Litigation, 45 Loy.U.Chi.L.J. 739, 752–53 (2014). Nevertheless, in the first half of 2017,
the filing of securities fraud class actions in federal court spiked, and was higher than at any other time since Congress enacted the PSLRA—more than
twice the 1996–2016 average. See Cornerstone Research, Securities Class Action Filings: 2017 Year in Review, at 1.
